state_background_check.value: No — Colorado disqualifies convicted felons from state office only during actual confinement or probation (automatically restored after), except a narrow list of crimes (embezzlement of public funds, bribery, perjury, solicitation of bribery, subornation of perjury) that carries permanent disqualification instead; but the U.S. Constitution's own qualifications for Congress (age, citizenship, residency) can't be added to by any state, so none of this reaches U.S. House or Senate candidates
state_background_check.snippet: C.R.S. § 18-1.3-401: "Every person convicted of a felony... shall be disqualified from holding any office of honor, trust, or profit under the laws of this state... during the actual time of confinement or commitment to imprisonment or release from actual confinement on conditions of probation. Upon his or her discharge after completion of service of his or her sentence or after service under probation, the right to hold any office of honor, trust, or profit shall be restored, except as provided in section 4 of article XII of the state constitution." Congressional qualifications are set exclusively by the U.S. Constitution, confirmed per https://www.everycrsreport.com/reports/R41946.html: "the Framers intended the Constitution to be the exclusive source of qualifications for Members of Congress, and that the Framers thereby 'divested' States of any power to add qualifications."

enacted_laws.title: CONVEY Act
enacted_laws.summary: Clifton Opportunities Now for Vibrant Economic Yields Act or the CONVEY Act This act directs the Bureau of Land Management to convey to Mesa County, Colorado, a parcel of land in Clifton for fair market value. The county must pay all costs associated with the conveyance, including any surveying costs. The proceeds from the conveyance must be deposited into the Federal Land Disposal Account and be available for expenditure.

bio_summary.value: Communities like ours are best served by representatives who show up to govern, not to perform. When leadership is rooted in moderation and independence, the focus shifts away from constant outrage and toward the everyday work of representation—listening to constituents, building coalitions, and delivering results that actually improve people’s lives. For places built on agriculture, small business, and tight-knit communities, effectiveness matters more than headlines.
